demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
I distract myself with something else
Talking with others about the event or its aftermath

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

issues.item: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Evaluation' implies a strong social-evaluative/shame-based concern about performance or appearance, but there are no corresponding Negative Appraisal items about blame, shame, incompetence, or fear of judgment, and the trauma type is accidentally causing serious injury to another rather than an evaluative/social humiliation trauma. This item is therefore hard to integrate with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
issues.explanation: 'Safe Seat Seeking' suggests a spatial/physical-danger trigger pattern (e.g., choosing exits or protected positions in public places), but the formulation explicitly has Triggers inactive and the rest of the profile is dominated by intrusive memory phenomena rather than situational cue-driven threat. This item does not fit well with the stated node structure.

vignette:
Megan had been a paramedic in the Midlands long enough to trust her hands more than her nerves, but the night she was called to a multi-vehicle collision on a rain-slick dual carriageway had left her with a memory she could never smooth into a normal story. A driver had clipped a barrier, spun into the path of another car, and in the confusion Megan and her partner worked on a young man pinned awkwardly in the back seat. She was trying to keep him still and talking while the dashboard light flickered across blood on the seatbelt, when she made the decision that she later replayed with brutal clarity: she told a colleague to cut a restraint before the scene was fully stabilized. The movement she thought would free him instead worsened an internal injury, and by the time the ambulance bay doors closed at hospital, the patient was deteriorating. Megan never stopped returning to that sequence in her mind, but it did not return as a full narrative. It came in sudden pieces, a flash of her gloved hand, the sound of metal snipping, the young man’s eyes widening, the harsh white of the resuscitation room. She described it as a handful of snapshots rather than a memory, each one vivid and separate, and when one of those fragments hit, it brought back the same terror she had felt on scene, as if her body were back in the corridor outside the A&E cubicle.

Afterward, she began to lean on whatever could blunt those moments before they arrived. Some evenings she drank more than she meant to after shifts; on other nights she took leftover medication that made her feel dulled enough to fall asleep without thinking. At home she threw herself into scrolling, housework, and television so she would not sit still long enough for her mind to wander. She avoided talking about the incident with her husband or her colleagues, not because she lacked words, but because any attempt to explain it seemed to open the door to the same terror and the same jagged images. Yet the more she used those strategies to get through the day, the less settled her mind became. The fragments began to intrude at odd times, and the fact that she was always trying not to think about them made them feel closer, as if they were waiting just under the surface. Megan came to fear that if she let herself remember even briefly, she would be flooded all over again, and that fear made her reach faster for drink, distraction, or silence the next time the images flickered into view.

That sense of being on the brink of another replay changed the way she moved through ordinary life. She became markedly more watchful, especially at night, when the house was dark and the world outside the bedroom felt uncertain. She checked locks, listened for sounds in the street, and found herself scanning the road when she was driving home from shift, as if danger might emerge in an instant. During the day she could sometimes settle, but night made her feel much less safe, and the vigilance she brought to sleeping, walking to the car, or answering late calls wore down her concentration. She missed parts of conversations, lost her place in paperwork, and had to reread simple notes at work. Even at the station, where she had once been quick and steady, she found herself straining to stay alert for the moment something went wrong.

The hard part for Megan was that the memory and the sense of threat fed one another. A flash of the collision would arrive without warning while she was halfway through a meal or standing in the kitchen, and her body would tense before she had even named what she was seeing. Afterward she would feel unsafe, especially after dark, and that watchfulness made her scan for signs that something terrible was about to happen, which in turn seemed to leave her more exposed to another fragment of the event breaking through. On nights when she drank to calm herself or took something to help her switch off, she might sleep more easily at first, but the next day the memory felt fuzzier and more intrusive, as if her mind could not hold it in place. The poorer her concentration became, the more mistakes she worried she might make on duty, and that anxiety fed back into the same sense that she was no longer fully in control of her own attention or her own safety. She had started declining social plans after shifts and would invent excuses not to be asked about work, because even a sympathetic question could send her mind back to the scene and set off hours of unease.

By the time Megan sought help, she was exhausted by trying to outrun the event she had lived through and the one she kept reliving in pieces. What brought her in was not only the drinking and the missed moments at work, but the growing fear that her hyperalert nights and the sudden flashes of terror were becoming her new normal. She wanted to know whether she could ever remember what happened without being dragged back into that same terror, and whether she could feel safe again when the lights went out.
